items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that some money [MATH: P_0] is deposited into a bank account. We know the bank balance [MATH: P] after [MATH: t] years is given by the formula

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
P &= P_0\left(1 + \dfrac r n \right)^{nt},
}]
where [MATH: r] is the annual interest rate, and [MATH: n] is the number of times payments are compounded per year.

Content:
Now suppose that we increase the number of compounding periods per year so that compounding occurs at every instant. We call this continuous compounding. When continuous compounding occurs, we can determine the balance [MATH: P] at time [MATH: t] using the continuously compounded growth equation, given by

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
P &= P_0e^{rt},
}]

Content:
where [MATH: e\approx 2.718] is Euler's number. We'll go into a little more detail regarding where this formula comes from at the end of the lesson.

Content:
For example, suppose that a company has [MATH: \[math]450\,000] in the bank and that the balance grows at an annual rate of [MATH: 4.5\%,] continuously compounded. Then, to calculate the bank balance [MATH: 5] years from now, we can use the continuously compounded growth equation.

Content:
In this situation, we have an initial balance [MATH: P_0= 450\,000,] a growth rate of [MATH: r= 4.5\% = 0.045,] and [MATH: t=5] years. Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
P &= P_0e^{rt} \[3pt]
&= (450\,000)e^{(0.045)(5)} \[3pt]
&= (450\,000)e^{0.225} \[3pt]
&= (450\,000)(1.252\,322\,716) \[3pt]
&\approx 563\,545.
}]

Content:
So, the balance in [MATH: 5] years will be approximately [MATH: \[/math]563\,545.]

Content:
The rate [MATH: r] in the continuously compounded growth equation does not have to be an annual rate. It can be over any amount of time. The time [MATH: t] inherits its unit from the rate.

sections.normalized_html: An asset has been depreciating in value for the past [MATH: 10] years at an annual, continuously-compounded rate of [MATH: 6\%.] If that asset was initially worth [MATH: \[math]13\,500,] what is it worth now? Round your answer to the nearest dollar.
sections.readable_text: An asset has been depreciating in value for the past [MATH: 10] years at an annual, continuously-compounded rate of [MATH: 6\%.] If that asset was initially worth [MATH: \[math]13\,500,] what is it worth now? Round your answer to the nearest dollar.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The continuously compounded growth equation is

[MATH: \eqalign{ P &= P_0e^{rt}. }]

We have an initial amount of [MATH: P_0=13\,500,] a rate of [MATH: r=-0.06,] and a time duration of [MATH: t=10] years. Substituting these values into the formula, we get

[MATH: \eqalign{ P &= P_0e^{rt} \ &= 13\,500e^{(-0.06)(10)} \[3pt] &= 13\,500e^{-0.6} \[3pt] &= 13\,500(0.548\,81...) \[3pt] &\approx 7\,409. }]

Therefore, after [MATH: 10] years, the value of the asset has decreased to [MATH: \[math]7\,409.]

[MATH: P|= P_{0}e^{rt}; 20500|= P_{0}e^{(0.052)(14)}; 20500|= P_{0}e^{0.728}; 20500|= P_{0}(2.07093...); P_{0}|= (20500)/(2.07093...); P_{0}|≈ 9899.]

Therefore, there were [MATH: 9\,899] bacteria initially.

Content:
The formula for continuously compounded growth, given by
[MATH: P=P_0 e^{rt}]

Content:
is actually equal to the compound interest equation

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
P &= P_0 \left(1 + \dfrac r n \right)^{nt},
}]

Content:
for extremely large [MATH: n] (in other words, as [MATH: n \rightarrow \infty]).

Content:
To demonstrate, let's take the case of [MATH: P_0=1,] [MATH: r=1,] and [MATH: t=1.] Then the formula for continuously compounded growth gives

Content:
[MATH: P|= P_{0}e^{1 ⋅ 1}; = 1e^{1 ⋅ 1}; = e; = 2.7182818…]

Content:
and the compound interest equation is

Content:
[MATH: P|= P_{0}(1 + (r)/(n))^{nt}; = 1(1 + (1)/(n))^{n ⋅ 1}; = (1 + (1)/(n))^{n}.]

Content:
If we substitute a large value of [MATH: n,] say [MATH: n=1\,000\,000,] then we get

Content:
[MATH: P|= (1 + (1)/(1000000))^{1000000}; = (1.000001)^{1000000}; ≈ 2.718280; ≈ e.]

Content:
This result matches up nicely with our result from the formula for continuously compounded growth!

Content:
Here, we demonstrated that the result holds for the special case where [MATH: P_0=r=t=1.] However, it is possible to show that the formula is always true.

Item 2 — Example: Calculating a Final Amount After Continuous Compounding Is Applied

Example Prompt:
An asset has been depreciating in value for the past [MATH: 10] years at an annual, continuously-compounded rate of [MATH: 6\%.] If that asset was initially worth [MATH: \[math]13\,500,] what is it worth now? Round your answer to the nearest dollar.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The continuously compounded growth equation is

[MATH: \eqalign{
P &= P_0e^{rt}.
}]

We have an initial amount of [MATH: P_0=13\,500,] a rate of [MATH: r=-0.06,] and a time duration of [MATH: t=10] years. Substituting these values into the formula, we get

[MATH: \eqalign{
P &= P_0e^{rt} \
&= 13\,500e^{(-0.06)(10)} \[3pt]
&= 13\,500e^{-0.6} \[3pt]
&= 13\,500(0.548\,81...) \[3pt]
&\approx 7\,409.
}]

Therefore, after [MATH: 10] years, the value of the asset has decreased to [MATH: \[math]7\,409.]

Explanation:
The continuously compounded growth equation is

[MATH: \eqalign{
P &= P_0e^{rt}.
}]

We have a final amount of [MATH: P=20\,500,] a rate of [MATH: r=0.052,] and a time duration of [MATH: t=14] days. Substituting these values into the formula and solving for [MATH: P_0,] we get

[MATH: P|= P_{0}e^{rt}; 20500|= P_{0}e^{(0.052)(14)}; 20500|= P_{0}e^{0.728}; 20500|= P_{0}(2.07093...); P_{0}|= (20500)/(2.07093...); P_{0}|≈ 9899.]

Therefore, there were [MATH: 9\,899] bacteria initially.

Item 8 — Example: Calculating a Rate or Time Duration

Example Prompt:
Nine years ago, an organization had [MATH: 4\,350] members. Today it has [MATH: 7\,210] members. What was its continuously compounded rate of growth during this nine-year period? Round your answer to [MATH: 1] decimal place.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The continuously compounded growth equation is

[MATH: P = P_0e^{rt}.]

We have an initial amount of [MATH: P_0=4\,350,] a final amount of [MATH: P=7\,210,] and a time duration of [MATH: t=9] years. Substituting these values into the formula and solving for [MATH: r,] we get

[MATH: P|= P_{0}e^{rt}; 7210|= (4350)e^{r(9)}; e^{9r}|= (7210)/(4350); e^{9r}|= 1.65747...; \ln (e^{9r})|= \ln (1.65747...); 9r|= 0.50529...; r|= 0.05614... ≈ 5.6%.]

Therefore, continuously compounded rate of growth is [MATH: 5.6\%.]

Item 11 — Tutorial: The Relationship Between Continuous Compounding and the Compound Interest Equation

Content:
The formula for continuously compounded growth, given by
[MATH: P=P_0 e^{rt}]

Content:
is actually equal to the compound interest equation

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
P &= P_0 \left(1 + \dfrac r n \right)^{nt},
}]

Content:
for extremely large [MATH: n] (in other words, as [MATH: n \rightarrow \infty]).

Content:
To demonstrate, let's take the case of [MATH: P_0=1,] [MATH: r=1,] and [MATH: t=1.] Then the formula for continuously compounded growth gives

Content:
[MATH: P|= P_{0}e^{1 ⋅ 1}; = 1e^{1 ⋅ 1}; = e; = 2.7182818…]

Content:
and the compound interest equation is

Content:
[MATH: P|= P_{0}(1 + (r)/(n))^{nt}; = 1(1 + (1)/(n))^{n ⋅ 1}; = (1 + (1)/(n))^{n}.]

Content:
If we substitute a large value of [MATH: n,] say [MATH: n=1\,000\,000,] then we get

Content:
[MATH: P|= (1 + (1)/(1000000))^{1000000}; = (1.000001)^{1000000}; ≈ 2.718280; ≈ e.]

Content:
This result matches up nicely with our result from the formula for continuously compounded growth!

Content:
Here, we demonstrated that the result holds for the special case where [MATH: P_0=r=t=1.] However, it is possible to show that the formula is always true.
